know that the characteristics of a reaction at dynamic equilibrium are: the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate; the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant

primer.text: You already know from Rates of Reaction how fast a reaction proceeds and what speeds it up or slows it down. That idea is the engine of this note, because equilibrium is not about reactions stopping but about two rates meeting. Here you will meet reversible reactions and the balanced, dynamic state they settle into inside a sealed container.

lessons.title: Dynamic equilibrium
lessons.opening: Some reactions can undo themselves: the products re-form the reactants as readily as the reactants form the products. This lesson defines the special state such a reaction settles into, called dynamic equilibrium, and the one condition it demands — a closed container. Two features mark that state, and they are the ones the exam asks for.
keyPoints: A reversible reaction is one that can run in both the forward and reverse directions.
Equilibrium is reached when the rates of the forward and reverse reactions become equal.
At equilibrium the molecules keep changing into each other, which is why it is called dynamic.
The concentrations of reactants and products stay constant while nothing else changes.
A closed system is required, so no species can leave the vessel and nothing can enter.

low.restatement: In a sealed container, a reversible reaction settles at the point where both directions run at the same speed, with steady concentrations.
low.analogy: Imagine a shop where customers enter and leave at the same pace: the queue never changes even though people are always moving through.
low.examPointer: Learn the two equilibrium features as a pair — equal rates and constant concentrations — because questions ask for both.

medium.restatement: Dynamic means nothing stops: forward and reverse reactions keep converting the molecules into each other at equal rates, so the composition holds steady unless temperature or pressure changes.
medium.analogy: It is like two escalators running against each other at equal speed: anyone riding stays level, yet nobody stands still.
medium.examPointer: Quote both features precisely; saying the concentrations are equal between the two sides is a different claim and is wrong.

check.stem: What does it mean for a reaction to be reversible?

options.text: It occurs in both directions, with the products able to reform the reactants
options.explanation: Both directions run; nothing about the reaction is one-way.

options.text: It can be undone only by changing the temperature
options.explanation: Reversibility is built into the reaction itself, not a switching condition.

options.text: It runs halfway and stops there permanently
options.explanation: Reversible reactions do not stop; equilibrium is a balance of ongoing reactions.

options.text: It produces the same amount of products as reactants
options.explanation: Amounts at equilibrium need not match; rates, not quantities, are equal.

check.stem: Why must equilibrium be reached in a closed container?

options.text: So none of the participating species can escape and nothing else can enter
options.explanation: The closed vessel keeps every participant present so the two reactions can balance.

options.text: To keep the pressure high enough for the reaction to start
options.explanation: Starting the reaction is not the issue; keeping every species in the vessel is.

options.text: To stop the products decomposing
options.explanation: Products decomposing is part of the reverse reaction, not something prevented.

options.text: To keep the temperature constant
options.explanation: The container blocks matter transfer; temperature control is a separate matter.

check.stem: The concentrations at equilibrium are constant. What does that mean?

options.text: Each concentration stays the same over time, though the two sides' amounts need not match
options.explanation: Constant means unchanging, not identical between reactants and products.

options.text: Reactant and product concentrations are equal to each other
options.explanation: Equality of concentrations is not required; only the rates are equal.

options.text: Both concentrations are zero because the reaction finished
options.explanation: The reaction has not stopped; both sides remain present.

options.text: The concentrations keep rising steadily
options.explanation: Rising is change; constant means no net change over time.

check.stem: Why is the equilibrium described as dynamic?

options.text: Because both reactions keep running constantly, converting molecules into each other at the same rate
options.explanation: Dynamic names the ongoing change that balances out.

options.text: Because the concentrations change slowly over time
options.explanation: Concentrations stay constant at equilibrium.

options.text: Because the reaction needs constant stirring or heating
options.explanation: No input is required; the balance maintains itself.

options.text: Because the molecules move faster once equilibrium is reached
options.explanation: Molecular speed is not the claim; the ongoing two-way reactions are.

check.stem: A leak develops in the reaction vessel and gas escapes. What happens to the equilibrium?

options.text: It is disturbed: escaping material means the system is no longer closed, so the balance cannot hold
options.explanation: The closed-system requirement is exactly about keeping everything in the vessel.

options.text: Nothing; equilibrium survives leaks because the rates stay equal anyway
options.explanation: With material leaving, the two rates can no longer stay matched.

options.text: The reaction immediately runs to completion
options.explanation: Loss of material unbalances the rates; it does not force completion.

options.text: The reaction reverses completely, leaving only reactants
options.explanation: Nothing forces total reversal; the balance is simply lost.

lessons.title: Reaching equilibrium: the Haber process
sourceHeadings: The rate of the forward and reverse reaction during the progress of a reaction
lessons.opening: Definitions become clearer when watched in motion, and the Haber process is the note's chosen showcase. It makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, and its rate story ends exactly at equilibrium. Follow the two rates from the start of the reaction and you can see the state assemble itself.
keyPoints: At the beginning, only nitrogen and hydrogen are present, so the forward rate is at its highest.
As the reaction proceeds, the nitrogen and hydrogen concentrations fall, and the forward rate falls with them.
The ammonia concentration rises, so the backward reaction speeds up, decomposing ammonia back into the reactants.
In the closed system the two rates eventually become equal, and equilibrium is reached.
The Haber process is the note's example of a reaction reaching equilibrium in a sealed container.

low.restatement: The forward rate starts highest and falls as nitrogen and hydrogen are used up, while the backward rate rises with the growing ammonia, until the two meet.
low.analogy: Picture two cars approaching from opposite ends of a road, one slowing and one speeding up, until they draw level and stay there.
low.examPointer: Sketching the two rate curves meeting is a classic mark; label the meeting point equilibrium.

medium.restatement: Rate tracks concentration: abundant nitrogen and hydrogen make the forward reaction fastest at the start, while rising ammonia strengthens the reverse reaction; in the closed vessel neither gas can escape, so the rates converge to equality.
medium.analogy: Think of two rival shops sharing one street: as one runs out of stock, its custom slows while the other's grows, until trade balances.
medium.examPointer: Explain why the curves flatten: equal rates mean each substance is made as fast as it is destroyed, not that the reaction has stopped.

check.stem: At the start of the Haber process, why is the forward rate at its highest?

options.text: Because the nitrogen and hydrogen concentrations are at their highest, and rate tracks concentration
options.explanation: The note's own reasoning: the most reactant present means the fastest forward reaction.

options.text: Because the ammonia is pushing the reaction forward
options.explanation: There is no ammonia at the start; only nitrogen and hydrogen are present.

options.text: Because the temperature is highest at the start
options.explanation: Temperature is held steady; the start's speed comes from abundant reactants.

options.text: Because the vessel is newest and cleanest
options.explanation: The rate is set by concentrations, not by vessel condition.

check.stem: Why does the forward rate fall as the reaction proceeds?

options.text: The nitrogen and hydrogen concentrations gradually decrease as they are consumed
options.explanation: Less reactant means fewer collisions, so the forward rate drops.

options.text: The nitrogen and hydrogen particles slow down over time
options.explanation: Particle speed is not the mechanism; concentration is.

options.text: The ammonia blocks the forward reaction from outside the vessel
options.explanation: Ammonia rises within the mixture; it does not act from outside.

options.text: The vessel walls absorb the gases
options.explanation: Nothing leaves a closed vessel; the fall is internal consumption.

check.stem: What happens to the backward reaction as ammonia accumulates?

options.text: It speeds up, because its reactant, ammonia, keeps increasing
options.explanation: The reverse reaction consumes ammonia, so more ammonia means a faster reverse rate.

options.text: It stays at zero until equilibrium is reached
options.explanation: The backward reaction begins as soon as ammonia exists.

options.text: It slows down, because the ammonia blocks it
options.explanation: More ammonia speeds the decomposition, it does not slow it.

options.text: It runs faster than the forward reaction until equilibrium
options.explanation: The backward rate rises to meet the forward one; the note has them becoming equal.

check.stem: Why do the two rates eventually become equal?

options.text: In the closed system the two reactions are interlinked and no gas can escape, so the rates settle at equality
options.explanation: The note's own account: interlinked reactions in a closed system converge.

options.text: Because the reaction runs out of energy and stops
options.explanation: Nothing stops; the rates match while both reactions continue.

options.text: Because the nitrogen and hydrogen have completely run out
options.explanation: Reactants are still present at equilibrium; their concentrations are constant, not zero.

options.text: Because the ammonia fills the vessel and forces a stop
options.explanation: Filling the vessel is not what balances the rates.

check.stem: At equilibrium in the Haber process, which statement is true?

options.text: The forward and reverse rates are equal, and the concentrations have stopped changing
options.explanation: That is exactly the pair of features the exam hint lists.

options.text: Both reactions have stopped, so the amounts are fixed
options.explanation: The reactions continue; the amounts are fixed by the equal rates.

options.text: The rate of making ammonia equals the total amount made
options.explanation: Rate compares with rate; it is not compared with an amount.

options.text: The concentrations of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia are all equal
options.explanation: Equal rates, not equal concentrations, is the equilibrium condition.

glossary.definition: A reaction that occurs in both directions, with the products able to reform the reactants.
The state reached when the forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate.
Actively changing; at equilibrium the molecules keep converting into each other at equal rates.
A setup where no substances can enter or leave the reaction vessel.
The amount of a substance held in a given volume of mixture.
The industrial reaction making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen; the note's equilibrium example.

workedExample.prompt: In the Haber process, nitrogen and hydrogen react reversibly to form ammonia in a sealed container. a) Describe how the forward and backward reaction rates change from the start until equilibrium. b) State the two characteristics of the reaction mixture at dynamic equilibrium. c) Why must the container be sealed?
steps: a) At the start only nitrogen and hydrogen are present, so the forward rate is at its highest; as their concentrations fall, the forward rate decreases.
Meanwhile the ammonia concentration rises, so the backward reaction speeds up, and the two rates eventually become equal — equilibrium is reached.
b) At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
c) A closed system means no chemical species can leave the vessel and nothing can enter; a leak would upset the balance, so equilibrium requires a sealed container.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Forward rate falls from its maximum while the backward rate rises, until they are equal. b) Equal forward/reverse rates; constant concentrations. c) Nothing may enter or leave the vessel.
